title: March of the Penguins
full_review:
Without question, the award for parents of the year goes to the webfooted wonders in "March of the Penguins" (Warner Independent), a nature documentary that chronicles the yearly mating migrations of emperor penguins in the Antarctic. It is also, to date, one of the best movies of the year.

To say that Luc Jacquet's remarkable film it is just a movie about penguins, is like saying that "Citizen Kane" is about a guy who sells newspapers.

Beautifully captured by Jacquet and his hearty crew, the odyssey has all the life-and-death peril of an adventure movie, but at its heart remains a grand romance, a saga where parental devotion and self-sacrifice overcome seemingly insurmountable obstacles to prove, as the film's tag line states, that "in the harshest place on Earth, love finds a way."

Their amazing journey begins each spring the same way it has for millennia, with the aquatic birds torpedoing themselves out of their natural home in the ocean and onto the unwelcoming ice to begin their procession inland.

Waddling in step -- or in some cases propelling themselves tummy-toboggan style -- the penguins, with their faux formal wear and distinctive orange-accented beaks and heads, cross 70 miles of the most inhospitable terrain on the planet, kept on course by some inner compass, before arriving at their semishielded breeding colony.

Once gathered, the penguins commence their mating ritual, using a combination of courtship dances and songs to couple. Though the penguins number in the thousands, each one has a unique "vocal signature" that allows easy identification by its partner.

Within two months of mating, the female lays an egg and gingerly hands it off to the male, a delicate procedure since contact with the frigid ice would spell almost instantaneous death to the chick within.

Having lost more than a third of their body weight, the females quickly start their return trek to the ocean -- made considerably longer and more treacherous by the encroaching winter's fury -- where, as they feast on fish, some fall prey to leopard seals.

Meanwhile, back in the rookery, the males stoically stand guard over the egg, balancing it on their feet as a buffer from the ice, for more than two months. Huddled together in rotating formation, they must endure hellish subzero temperatures and starvation, forgoing food until the females return in late July.

Reminiscent of "Winged Migration" in the poeticism of its wordless storytelling, the film is as emotionally gripping as it is visually spectacular.

Among the film's many highlights is a tender moment when proud parents are reunited over a chirping bundle of fluff.

Jacquet captures emotions ranging from the comic (penguins belly-flopping across the ice); to the tragic (a heartbreaking scene of a mother "grieving" the loss of her chick); to the heroic (a phalanx of males braving a brutal blizzard). At times they almost seem human.

Those curious about how the filmmakers were able to get such astonishing up-close images should stick around for the closing credits, which include behind-the-scenes footage.

The fablelike feel of the film is enhanced by Morgan Freeman's cadenced, warm-toned narration.

"March of the Penguins" is the perfect antidote for the cinematic junk food packaged as entertainment during summer months.

And while cynics may dismiss such sentimentality as inferring emotion into a simple biological drive to reproduce, this captivating family film (in the best sense of the word) imparts a heart-warming message that, to borrow a phrase from St. Paul, "Love endures all things."

The film contains a brief predatory image and some sad moments. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audience.
